title: Digital Marketing Fundamentals for Small Businesses
subtitle: Plan, run and measure simple digital marketing that brings real customers to your small business, using search, social media, email and WhatsApp.
description: A practical course for Nigerian and African small business owners. You will define your target customer, set up your core online channels, get found on Google, plan useful content, sell through WhatsApp, run small paid ads, and calculate whether your marketing is making money.
outcomes: Define a target customer and write a clear value proposition
Set up a consistent digital presence on WhatsApp Business, Google Business Profile and one social platform
Plan a content calendar and organise WhatsApp sales with catalog, labels and broadcasts
Plan and run a small campaign with a written brief and a budget
Calculate reach, click-through rate, conversion rate, cost per result and ROAS, and judge profit against break-even
Improve results with A/B tests and repeat-customer strategies
audience: Women who run or plan a small business and want more customers from their phone, with basic smartphone and WhatsApp skills.
tools: A Google account for Google Business Profile and Google Sheets (free)
A Facebook page or Instagram professional account (free)
Optional: a small ad budget you can afford to lose while learning

modules.title: Foundations: customers, channels and a plan
modules.overview: Before you post or pay for anything, you need three things: a clear picture of who buys from you, a small set of online places where they can find you, and a goal with numbers attached. This module builds all three, using the marketing funnel as the map for the whole course.

lessons.title: Digital vs traditional marketing and the marketing funnel
objectives: Compare digital and traditional marketing on cost, targeting and measurement
Sort your marketing channels into owned, earned and paid media
Describe the four stages of the marketing funnel
Calculate the cost of reaching 1,000 people on two different channels

blocks.text: **Marketing** is everything you do to help the right people discover your product, trust it, buy it and come back. **Traditional marketing** uses offline channels: flyers, banners, radio jingles, newspaper adverts, posters at the bus stop and word of mouth in the market. **Digital marketing** uses the internet and mobile phones: search engines such as Google, social media such as Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, email, WhatsApp, and online maps.

blocks.name: marketing
blocks.alt: A woman standing beside a large megaphone and marketing charts
blocks.caption: Marketing, online or offline, is about helping the right customer find you and choose you.

blocks.text: Digital does not replace traditional. A woman selling fabrics at Balogun Market still gains customers who walk past her stall. But digital adds three powers that a flyer does not have. First, **targeting**: you can show an advert only to people in Ibadan who are interested in weddings, instead of everyone who passes a pole. Second, **measurement**: you can see how many people saw your post, how many clicked and how many sent a message. Third, **low starting cost**: a WhatsApp Business account and a Google Business Profile are free to create, so a small business can start with only data and time.
Owned, earned and paid media
Marketers group channels into three families. Knowing which family a channel belongs to helps you decide where to spend time and where to spend money.

head: Type
What it means
Examples for a small business
Main cost
rows: WhatsApp Business catalog, your website, your email list, your Facebook page
Attention other people give you for free
Customer reviews on Google, a customer sharing your post, a blogger mentioning you
Facebook and Instagram ads, Google Ads, paying an influencer
Money, charged per view or per click

blocks.text: A healthy plan uses all three. Owned channels are your shop window that nobody can take away. Earned media is the most trusted, because it comes from other customers. Paid media is the fastest way to reach new people, but it stops the moment you stop paying. Many small businesses make the mistake of paying for ads before their owned channels are ready, so new visitors arrive at an empty page and leave.
The marketing funnel

The **marketing funnel** describes the journey from a stranger to a loyal customer. It is wide at the top, because many people hear about you, and narrow at the bottom, because only some of them buy. This course uses a simple four-stage version.

blocks.title: The four-stage marketing funnel
items: Awareness: they discover you
Consideration: they compare and ask
Conversion: they buy
Loyalty: they return and refer
blocks.caption: Each stage needs different content and a different measure of success.

items: **Awareness**: a person sees your post, your advert or your shop on Google Maps for the first time. You measure reach: how many people saw you.
**Consideration**: she looks at your catalog, reads reviews, asks the price on WhatsApp. You measure clicks, profile visits and messages.
**Conversion**: she pays, by transfer, POS or a payment link from Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint. You measure orders and sales.
**Loyalty**: she buys again and tells her friends. You measure repeat orders and referrals.

blocks.text: When sales are low, the funnel helps you find where the problem is. If many people see your posts but nobody messages, the problem is in consideration: perhaps your price is hidden or your photos are poor. If many people message but few pay, the problem is in conversion: perhaps you reply too slowly or delivery is unclear.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing the cost of reaching people
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sells small chops for parties in Port Harcourt. She has two options for a weekend promotion. All prices are illustrative and approximate.
steps: Option A: print 500 flyers for about ₦15,000 and pay a helper about ₦5,000 to share them. Total about ₦20,000. If every flyer reaches one person, she reaches 500 people.
Cost per 1,000 people for flyers: ₦20,000 ÷ 500 × 1,000 = ₦40,000.
Option B: run a Facebook and Instagram ad for about ₦10,000. Her Ads Manager report later shows a reach of 8,000 people in Port Harcourt.
She also checks results: the flyers brought 3 orders that she can trace (she asked each caller where they heard of her), and the ad brought 5 orders through WhatsApp.
blocks.result: The ad reached far more people for each naira, and she could measure it directly. The flyers still worked locally, so she keeps a few for her own street and moves most of her budget to the ad. Your numbers will differ: the lesson is the method, not the figures.

blocks.title: Reach is not sales
blocks.text: Cheap reach only matters if the right people see you. 8,000 people who never throw parties are worth less than 300 who do. Always follow the funnel down to messages and orders before you decide a channel is working.

takeaways: Digital marketing adds targeting, measurement and a low starting cost to traditional methods.
Owned, earned and paid media work best together; build owned channels first.
The funnel runs from awareness to consideration, conversion and loyalty.
Cost per 1,000 people reached = cost ÷ people reached × 1,000.

activity.title: Map your current marketing
steps: List every way customers currently hear about your business, online and offline.
Label each one owned, earned or paid.
For each, write which funnel stage it mainly serves.
Circle the funnel stage that has no channel at all. That is your first gap.
activity.evidence: A one-page table or notebook photo of your channels, labelled by media type and funnel stage.

lessons.title: Defining your target customer
objectives: Explain why marketing to 'everybody' wastes money
Describe a target customer using demographics, location, needs and habits
Write a short customer profile and a one-line value proposition
Plan five short customer interviews

blocks.text: Your **target customer** is the specific kind of person most likely to buy from you and come back. Many small business owners say, 'My product is for everybody.' It may be true that anyone can use it, but you cannot afford to speak to everybody. Advertising platforms charge for every view, and a message written for everyone usually speaks to no one.

blocks.name: target-audience
blocks.alt: A person pointing at a group of selected customer profiles
blocks.caption: Choosing one clear customer group makes every post and advert sharper.

blocks.text: Four lenses for describing a customer

head: Lens
Questions to answer
Example answers
rows: Age range, gender, job, family situation, income level
Women 28 to 45, working mothers, salaried or trading
Where do they live, work and shop? How far will you deliver?
Within Lekki and Ajah, delivery under one hour
What problem does your product solve? What do they worry about?
No time to cook healthy meals on weekdays
Which apps do they use? When are they online? How do they pay?
WhatsApp all day, Instagram at night, pay by transfer

blocks.text: The last lens matters most for digital marketing. If your customers are traders in their 50s who live on WhatsApp and Facebook, a TikTok strategy will waste your energy. If they are university students, the opposite may be true. Do not guess: ask them.
Write a customer profile

A **customer profile** (marketers also call it a **persona**) is a short description of one typical buyer, written as if she were a real person. It keeps your posts consistent, because every time you write a caption you can ask, 'Would she care about this?' Base it on real conversations with your best customers, not on imagination.

blocks.title: Worked example: a customer profile for a meal-prep business
blocks.context: For example, Bisi cooks weekly meal packs in Abuja. She looks at her last 30 orders on WhatsApp and talks to six regular customers.
steps: She notices 22 of the 30 orders came from women, most of them working in offices in Wuse and Garki.
In conversations, four of six say their biggest problem is coming home too tired to cook, and worrying that the family eats too much fast food.
Most order on Sunday evening after seeing her WhatsApp Status, and pay by bank transfer.

She writes the profile: 'Chioma, 34, works in an office in Wuse, two children, leaves home at 6:30am. Wants her family to eat home-style food on weekdays without cooking every night. Checks WhatsApp Status on Sunday evenings. Pays by transfer. Worries about hygiene and freshness.'
She writes her value proposition: 'Home-style Nigerian meals for busy Abuja families, cooked fresh on Sunday and delivered to your door.'
blocks.result: Bisi now posts her weekly menu on Sunday afternoon, shows her clean kitchen and packaging to answer the hygiene worry, and stops spending on adverts aimed at students who rarely order.

blocks.text: The value proposition

A **value proposition** is one sentence that says who you help, what you give them and why you are different. A useful pattern is: '[Product] for [target customer] who want [result], [what makes you different].' Avoid empty words such as 'quality' and 'best' unless you prove them. 'Delivered within 2 hours in Ikeja' is stronger than 'fast delivery'.
Talk to five customers

The fastest research is a short conversation, by phone or WhatsApp voice note, with five customers who have bought before. Keep it to about ten minutes. Ask open questions and listen more than you speak. Write their exact words down, because those words make the best captions later.

blocks.title: Five questions for a customer interview
items: How did you find us?
Why did you buy?
What nearly stopped you?
Where else did you look?
Who else should know?
blocks.caption: These five questions reveal your best channel, your real selling point, your main objection and your referral path.

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: Ask permission before you record a call or quote a customer by name in a post. Keep customer phone numbers and addresses private and use them only for the purpose you collected them for. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires businesses to handle personal data lawfully and securely.

You may find you have two or three groups, for example individual buyers and small shops that resell. That is fine. Write one profile for each, then choose one as your main focus for the next three months. You can expand later once the first group is working.
Common mistakes when defining customers

items: **Describing yourself instead of the buyer.** You may love bright colours, but your best buyers may prefer muted corporate styles. Let the orders decide.
**Choosing a group you cannot reach.** If you only deliver within Kaduna, a customer profile in Lagos is no use, however attractive.
**Never updating it.** Review your profile every few months. Customers change, and so do their favourite apps.
**Ignoring who pays.** For school uniforms, the child wears it but the parent pays. Speak to the person who makes the decision.

takeaways: Marketing to everybody wastes money; pick a specific target customer.
Describe customers by demographics, location, needs and online habits.
Base your customer profile on real orders and real conversations.
A value proposition says who you help, with what result, and why you are different.

activity.title: Build your customer profile
steps: Look through your last 20 to 30 sales and note any patterns in who bought.
Interview at least three customers using the five questions.
Write a customer profile of 60 to 100 words for your main customer group.
Write a one-sentence value proposition using the pattern in this lesson.
activity.evidence: Your written customer profile, value proposition and interview notes.

lessons.title: Building your digital presence: the starter kit
objectives: Choose the core online channels a small business needs first
Set up a WhatsApp Business profile with complete business details
Keep your business name, address and phone number consistent everywhere
Plan a simple link page or website that points to all your channels

blocks.text: Your **digital presence** is everything a customer finds when she looks for you online. Before you run adverts, make sure this presence is complete and trustworthy. Think of it as cleaning and stocking your shop before you invite people in. For most small businesses in Nigeria, the starter kit has four parts.

blocks.name: mobile-marketing
blocks.alt: A large phone screen showing a shop profile with products and a message button
blocks.caption: For most of your customers, your digital presence is what they see on a phone screen.

blocks.title: How the starter kit connects
items: Social page attracts
Google profile gets found
Link page connects all
WhatsApp closes the sale
blocks.caption: Each channel sends customers towards the place where you take orders.

blocks.text: 1. WhatsApp Business

**WhatsApp Business** is a free app from Meta, separate from ordinary WhatsApp, designed for small businesses. It lets you create a business profile with your address, hours, description, email and website, a **catalog** of products with photos and prices, automatic **greeting** and **away messages**, **quick replies** for common answers, and **labels** to sort customers. You can move your existing number to it, and your chats come with you. Lesson 3.4 covers it in depth.
2. Google Business Profile

A **Google Business Profile** is the free listing that appears on Google Search and Google Maps when someone searches for your business or for a service 'near me'. It shows your location or service area, phone number, hours, photos and reviews. Even home-based businesses can list a service area instead of a street address. Lesson 2.2 walks through it step by step.
3. One main social media page

Choose one platform where your target customer already spends time, usually Facebook, Instagram or TikTok, and do it well before adding a second. A business page on Facebook or a professional account on Instagram gives you free statistics (often called **insights**) and the ability to run ads later.
4. A link page or simple website

A website is not compulsory on day one, but you need one link that gathers everything. Options include a free link page, a simple site from a builder such as Google Sites or WordPress.com, or a store page from a payment provider. A website you control is owned media: no platform can suspend it. WhatsApp also gives every number a short link in the form wa.me/234XXXXXXXXXX (country code, then the number without the first zero), which opens a chat with you directly.
Consistency builds trust

Use exactly the same **business name, address and phone number** (marketers call this **NAP**) on every channel. If your Instagram says 'Tola's Kitchen', Google says 'Tolas Catering Services' and WhatsApp shows a different number, customers become unsure, and Google finds it harder to confirm your details. Use the same logo, colours and description everywhere too.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up the kit for a tailoring business
blocks.context: For example, Funke runs a tailoring shop in Ogbomosho and currently uses only her personal WhatsApp.
steps: Day 1: She installs WhatsApp Business on her phone and moves her number to it. She adds the shop name 'Funke Stitches', the category Clothing, her address, opening hours 9am to 6pm Monday to Saturday, and a description: 'Ankara, aso ebi and corporate wear made to measure in Ogbomosho. Ready in 7 days.'
Day 2: She photographs 12 finished outfits in daylight against a plain wall and adds them to her catalog with price ranges, for example 'Ankara gown from about ₦18,000'.
Day 3: She creates a Google Business Profile with the same name, address and phone number, adds the same photos and her hours, and requests verification.
Day 4: She converts her Instagram account to a professional account, uses the same name and logo, and puts her wa.me link in the bio.
Day 5: She asks five happy customers to leave an honest Google review.
blocks.result: In under a week Funke has a consistent presence: customers who find her on Instagram or Google can tap straight into a WhatsApp chat, see her catalog and know her hours before they ask.

blocks.title: Protect your accounts
blocks.text: Turn on two-step verification in WhatsApp settings and on your Facebook and Google accounts. Never share a verification code (OTP) with anyone, even someone claiming to be from Meta or Google. Anyone who gets your code can take over your account.

Finally, look at your presence as a stranger would. Search your business name on Google, open your profile on someone else's phone, and check every link. If anything is missing or out of date, fix it before you spend a single naira on promotion.

blocks.title: Good product photos on a phone
blocks.text: Shoot near a window in daylight, not under a yellow bulb. Use a plain background such as a white wall or a clean cloth. Wipe the camera lens first, hold the phone steady with both hands, and take the same angle for every product so your catalog looks tidy. Show size by placing the item next to something familiar, such as a hand.

takeaways: The starter kit: WhatsApp Business, Google Business Profile, one social page and one link that connects them.
Complete every profile field: hours, address or service area, description and photos.
Keep name, address and phone number identical everywhere.
Turn on two-step verification and never share OTP codes.

activity.title: Audit and complete your starter kit
steps: Search your business name on Google and note what appears.
Set up or update your WhatsApp Business profile with every field filled.
Check that your name, address and phone number match on all channels.
Create your wa.me link and add it to your social bio.
Turn on two-step verification on each account.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your completed WhatsApp Business profile and social bio, and a note of your NAP details.

lessons.title: Setting SMART goals and a 90-day marketing plan
objectives: Turn a business goal into a marketing goal with a number and a deadline
Write goals using the SMART test
Work backwards through the funnel to estimate how many people you must reach
Draft a one-page 90-day plan with a budget

blocks.text: 'I want more customers' is a wish, not a goal. A goal needs a number, a time and a way to check it. Goals turn marketing from guesswork into something you can measure and improve. This lesson gives you a method to set goals and to calculate what it will take to reach them.

blocks.name: goals
blocks.alt: A woman checking items off a goals board
blocks.caption: Clear goals with numbers let you see whether your marketing is working.

blocks.text: The SMART test

head: Letter
Meaning
Weak version
Strong version
rows: Achievable: realistic for your time and money?
Relevant: does it serve the business?

blocks.text: Followers and likes feel good but do not pay rent. Marketers call numbers that look impressive but do not connect to sales **vanity metrics**. Keep them, but make your main goal about something closer to money: orders, bookings, enquiries or repeat customers.
Work backwards through the funnel

Once you have a sales goal, you can estimate how many people you need at each funnel stage. You need two numbers from your own history: what share of people who **message** you end up **buying**, and what share of people who **see** your content end up **messaging**. These shares are called **conversion rates**. If you have never measured them, track them for two weeks first, using tally marks in a notebook if needed.

blocks.title: From goal back to reach
items: 40 orders (goal)
200 WhatsApp chats
10,000 people reached
blocks.caption: Dividing the goal by each conversion rate tells you how wide the top of the funnel must be.

blocks.title: Worked example: how many people must Bisi reach?
blocks.context: For example, Bisi (the Abuja meal-prep seller) wants 40 orders in March. Her notebook from February shows: of every 100 people who chatted with her, 20 ordered. Her Status and Facebook insights suggest about 2 of every 100 people who see her posts send a message.
steps: Chat-to-order conversion rate = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
Chats needed = 40 orders ÷ 0.20 = 200 chats.
View-to-chat conversion rate = 2 ÷ 100 = 2%.
People to reach = 200 chats ÷ 0.02 = 10,000 people in March.
Her free posts reach about 4,000 people a month, so she needs about 6,000 more. She plans a small paid campaign and asks happy customers to share her menu.
blocks.result: Bisi now knows the size of the job. She also sees a cheaper route: if she raises her chat-to-order rate from 20% to 25% by replying faster and showing delivery times clearly, she needs only 160 chats and 8,000 people reached.

blocks.title: Improve the bottom first
blocks.text: It is usually cheaper to improve conversion (faster replies, clear prices, easy payment) than to buy more reach. Fix the leaks at the bottom of the funnel before pouring more people in at the top.
Your one-page 90-day plan

items: Goal: one SMART goal for the next 90 days.
Customer: one line from your customer profile.
Channels: two or three channels, each linked to a funnel stage.
Content and actions: what you will post or do each week, for example three posts and two Status updates weekly.
Budget: money for ads, data and printing, and hours per week. Spend only what you can afford to lose while you learn.
Measures: which numbers you will record each week and where (a notebook, Google Sheets or Excel).

blocks.text: Split 90 days into three months. Month one: build and test. Month two: keep what works and drop what does not. Month three: put more effort and money into the winners. Review your numbers every week, even for ten minutes, and write one sentence about what you learned.
Setting a sensible budget

There is no correct amount to spend on marketing. Start from what one customer is worth to you. If a meal pack earns Bisi about ₦3,000 profit after ingredients, packaging and delivery (an illustrative figure), she cannot spend more than ₦3,000 in advertising to win one order, or she loses money on it. In practice she should aim for much less, so the business still makes a profit. Lesson 4.3 calls this the **break-even cost per result**.

Count your free resources too. Time spent posting, replying and photographing is a real cost. If you can give marketing only five hours a week, plan for two channels done well, not five done badly. Write the hours into your plan next to the naira, and protect them in your week like a customer appointment.

head: Plan item
Bisi's example
rows: WhatsApp Status (consideration), Facebook page (awareness), WhatsApp chat (conversion)
Menu post every Sunday, 3 Status updates, reply to chats within 30 minutes
About ₦15,000 for ads in March, plus 5 hours a week
People reached, chats, orders, repeat orders

takeaways: A SMART goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Focus goals on orders, enquiries and repeat customers, not vanity metrics.
Divide your sales goal by your conversion rates to find the reach you need.
Improving conversion is often cheaper than buying more reach.

activity.title: Write your 90-day plan
steps: Write one SMART sales goal for the next 90 days.
Estimate your chat-to-order and view-to-chat rates from recent records.
Calculate the chats and reach you need, showing your working.
Complete the six parts of the one-page plan, including a budget you can afford.
activity.evidence: Your one-page 90-day plan with the funnel calculation shown.

quiz.q: Kemi's Instagram posts reach about 5,000 people a week, but almost nobody sends a message. Which funnel stage most needs attention?
quiz.explain: Reach (awareness) is fine. People are seeing her but not taking the next step, so the problem is in consideration: unclear prices, weak photos or no easy way to message.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of earned media?
quiz.explain: Earned media is attention other people give you for free, such as reviews and shares. Ads are paid; catalogs and websites are owned.

quiz.q: An ad cost ₦6,000 and reached 4,000 people. What was the cost per 1,000 people reached?
Which goal passes the SMART test best?
options: Become the biggest cake brand in Lagos
Receive 30 cake orders through WhatsApp by 30 June
quiz.explain: It is specific (cake orders via WhatsApp), measurable (30), relevant to sales and time-bound (30 June). Posting daily is an activity, not a result.

quiz.q: Ada wants 30 orders. 15% of her chats become orders. About how many chats does she need?
quiz.explain: Chats needed = 30 ÷ 0.15 = 200.

quiz.q: Why should name, address and phone number be identical on WhatsApp, Google and social media?
options: Because it is required to post ads
It builds customer trust and helps Google confirm your details
It makes your posts reach more people automatically
It lowers the cost of data
quiz.explain: Consistent details reassure customers and help search engines trust that the listing is accurate.

modules.title: Search, local visibility and analytics
modules.overview: Customers who search are already looking for what you sell, which makes search the warmest traffic you can get. This module explains how search engines decide what to show, how to appear on Google Maps, how paid search works, and how to measure what your marketing is really producing.

lessons.title: How search engines work and how to be found
objectives: Explain crawling, indexing and ranking in plain words
Identify the four common types of search intent
Build a short keyword list using free Google tools
Improve a web page or profile with basic on-page search practice

blocks.text: When a customer types 'aso ebi tailor in Ibadan' into Google, she gets a list of results in less than a second. Google does not search the whole internet at that moment. It searches its own giant library, called the **index**, which it has built in advance. Understanding how that library is built helps you get into it, and then rise towards the top. The general practice of earning better positions in free search results is called **search engine optimisation**, or **SEO**.

blocks.name: search-engines
blocks.alt: A person in front of a large search bar and result cards
blocks.caption: Search engines match what people type with the pages in their index.

blocks.text: Three stages: crawl, index, serve

blocks.title: How Google Search works
items: Crawl: bots discover pages
Index: pages are stored and understood
Serve: best matches are ranked
Click: searcher visits you
blocks.caption: Google describes these three stages in its own Search Central documentation.

items: **Crawling**: automated programs (Google's is called Googlebot) follow links from page to page and download what they find. A page that no other page links to, and that is not submitted to Google, may never be found.
**Indexing**: Google reads the text, images and structure of each page and stores what it is about. Pages that are blocked, very thin or duplicated may be left out.

**Serving and ranking**: when someone searches, Google picks the pages from its index it judges most relevant and useful, considering things like the words used, the searcher's location and language, the quality of the page and how well it works on a phone.

blocks.text: Search intent: what is the searcher trying to do?

head: Intent
What the person wants
Example search
What to give them
rows: A complete Google profile and website
best bakery for wedding cakes in Enugu
Clear price, phone number, order button

blocks.text: Small businesses usually win most easily on searches that include a **location** and a **specific product**, because big national brands do not compete hard for them. 'Cake' is impossible to win; 'birthday cake delivery Ikeja' is realistic.
Finding your keywords for free

**Keywords** are the words and phrases people type. Find them the way your customer would. Start typing your product into Google and note the suggestions that appear below the box (Google Autocomplete). Scroll down the results page for 'People also ask' and related searches. Ask customers what they would type. If you later open a Google Ads account, its free **Keyword Planner** tool shows rough search volumes.

blocks.title: Worked example: a keyword list for a cake business
blocks.context: For example, Ronke bakes cakes from home in Ikeja, Lagos, and wants her simple website and Google profile to be found.
steps: She types 'birthday cake' into Google on her phone and notes suggestions such as 'birthday cake delivery' and 'birthday cake near me'.
She adds her area to each idea: 'birthday cake delivery Ikeja', 'custom cakes Ikeja', 'wedding cake Lagos'.
She asks five customers what they searched before finding her. Two say 'cake vendor in Ikeja', a phrase she had not thought of.
She chooses one main phrase per page: home page 'custom cakes in Ikeja', a second page 'wedding cakes in Lagos'.
She writes each page title, for example 'Custom Birthday Cakes in Ikeja | Ronke's Bakes', and uses the phrase naturally in the first paragraph and a photo caption.
blocks.result: Each page now has a clear topic matching real searches. Ronke avoids stuffing the same phrase into every sentence, which reads badly and does not help.

blocks.text: Basic on-page practice

items: Give every page a clear, unique **title** that includes the main phrase and your business name.
Write a short **description** (the summary under the title in results). Google may rewrite it, but a good one often gets used.
Use headings that say what each section is about, and write for people first.
Make sure the site works well on a phone and loads quickly on a slow connection: compress large photos before uploading.
Name photos sensibly (wedding-cake-ikeja.jpg, not IMG_2048.jpg) and add alt text describing them.
Register your site in **Google Search Console**, a free Google tool that shows which searches bring you visitors and flags problems.

blocks.title: Avoid shortcuts
blocks.text: Be wary of anyone who promises 'number one on Google in a week'. Buying links, copying other sites' text or hiding keywords can get pages pushed down or removed from results. Good SEO is slow and steady: useful pages, accurate details, real reviews.

If you have no website yet, the same ideas still apply to the places you do have. Your Google Business Profile description, your Facebook page 'About' section and your YouTube video titles are all read by search engines. Use the words your customers use, name your town, and describe exactly what you sell. 'Ankara gowns, aso ebi and school uniforms sewn in Ogbomosho' tells both people and search engines far more than 'Fashion is life'.

takeaways: Google crawls, indexes and then ranks pages; a page must be found before it can rank.
Match your content to search intent: learn, find, compare or buy.
Local, specific phrases are the easiest for small businesses to win.
Clear titles, phone-friendly pages and Search Console are the basics.

activity.title: Build your keyword list
steps: Type your main product into Google and write down at least five Autocomplete suggestions.
Add your town or area to each to make local phrases.
Ask two customers what they would search to find you.
Choose one main phrase for your home page or profile description and rewrite its title using it.
activity.evidence: Your keyword list of 8 to 10 phrases and your rewritten page title or profile description.

lessons.title: Google Business Profile and local search
objectives: Create and verify a Google Business Profile
Complete the profile fields that matter most for local results
Explain Google's three local ranking factors: relevance, distance and prominence
Ask for and respond to reviews honestly

blocks.text: When someone searches 'pharmacy near me' or 'hair salon Surulere', Google often shows a map with three businesses under it before the normal results. Those listings come from **Google Business Profile**, a free tool from Google. For shops, salons, restaurants, schools, clinics, artisans and service businesses, it can bring calls and direction requests from people who are ready to buy today.

blocks.name: location-search
blocks.alt: A person searching a map on a phone with location pins
blocks.caption: Local searchers are often ready to visit or call within hours.

blocks.text: Setting up your profile

items: Go to google.com/business on a browser, or open Google Maps and choose to add your business. Sign in with a Google account you will keep for the business.
Enter your business name exactly as customers see it on your signboard. Do not add extra keywords to the name; Google's guidelines forbid it.
Choose the most accurate **primary category**, for example 'Bakery' or 'Tailor'. You can add a few secondary categories.
Add your address if customers visit you. If you deliver or visit customers and work from home, hide the address and set a **service area** instead.
Add your phone number, your website or wa.me link, and your hours.

**Verify** the profile. Google offers different methods depending on the business, such as a phone or email code or a short video showing your location, signage and equipment. Your profile shows publicly only after verification.

blocks.text: Complete the profile fully

After verification, fill in everything: a description in plain language, products or services with prices where possible, opening hours including public holiday changes, and plenty of real photos. Add photos of the outside of the premises so people can recognise it, the inside, your team at work and your products. Use **posts** to share offers and news; they appear on your profile. Keep everything accurate: wrong hours are one of the quickest ways to lose a customer's trust.
How Google ranks local results

blocks.title: Google's three local ranking factors
items: Relevance: matches the search
Distance: close to the searcher
Prominence: well known and reviewed
blocks.caption: Google's own help pages name these three factors for local results.

blocks.text: You cannot change **distance**, but you can improve the other two. **Relevance** improves when your category, description, products and services clearly match what people search. **Prominence** grows with reviews, ratings, photos and how well known your business is across the web, including links and mentions from other sites and directories.
Reviews: ask, respond, never fake

Reviews help both ranking and trust. In your profile you can copy a short link that takes customers straight to the review form. Send it to happy customers after delivery, with a simple message. Respond to every review, good or bad, politely and within a few days.

blocks.title: Worked example: asking for and answering reviews
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs a hair salon in Kano. She has 4 reviews and wants more.
steps: After each appointment where the client seems happy, she sends on WhatsApp: 'Thank you for coming today! If you were happy with your hair, would you mind leaving us a short Google review? It helps other women find us: [review link].'
Over a month, about 1 in 4 clients she asks leaves a review. She asked 48 clients, so she gains about 12 reviews, taking her from 4 to 16.

One client leaves 2 stars, saying she waited 40 minutes. Halima replies: 'Thank you for telling us, Zainab. You are right that you waited too long, and we are sorry. We now confirm appointment times by WhatsApp the evening before. We would love to welcome you back.'
She checks her profile performance figures monthly: calls, direction requests and website clicks.
blocks.result: Halima's review count quadrupled with honest asking, and her calm reply to the negative review shows future clients that she listens. Many people read replies before choosing a business.

blocks.title: Fake and paid reviews break the rules
blocks.text: Do not write reviews for yourself, ask family to pretend to be customers, buy reviews, or offer discounts in exchange for reviews. Google's content policies prohibit fake engagement and incentivised reviews, and it can remove reviews or restrict profiles that break them. Also do not attack competitors with false reviews.
Using your profile performance data

Your profile shows how many people viewed it, and how many called, asked for directions or clicked to your website. Compare these with your sales. If views rise but calls stay flat, your photos, hours or description may not be convincing. If direction requests are high but few people arrive, check that your map pin is in the right place, and add a landmark to your description, such as 'opposite the First Bank on Allen Avenue'.

Finally, add your profile link to your WhatsApp Business profile, social bios and receipts, and check your profile at least once a month. Anyone can suggest edits to a public listing, so make sure your details have not been changed without your knowledge.

takeaways: Google Business Profile is free and puts you on Google Search and Maps.
Use your real business name, the right category, accurate hours and real photos.
Local ranking depends on relevance, distance and prominence.
Ask happy customers for reviews and reply to all reviews; never fake or pay for them.

activity.title: Create or improve your profile
steps: Search for your business on Google Maps to see if a listing already exists, then claim it or create one.
Fill in category, hours, description, contact details and at least 10 photos.
Copy your review link and send it to five recent happy customers.
Reply to every review you receive this week.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your completed profile and a note of reviews before and after.

lessons.title: Paid search basics with Google Ads
objectives: Explain how pay-per-click search ads and the ad auction work
Choose keywords, match types and negative keywords
Write a search ad that matches the searcher's intent
Calculate clicks, cost per click and cost per order from a budget

blocks.text: SEO and Google Business Profile bring free visitors, but they take time. **Paid search** lets you appear at the top of results quickly by paying Google. The ads are marked 'Sponsored' and look similar to normal results. With Google Ads you usually pay only when someone **clicks**, which is why it is called **pay per click** (PPC).

blocks.name: online-ad
blocks.alt: A screen showing an online advert with a click cursor
blocks.caption: Search ads appear when people type the words you choose.

blocks.text: How the ad auction works

Every time someone searches, Google runs a quick **auction** among advertisers who chose matching keywords. It does not simply give the top place to the highest bidder. Google considers your maximum bid, the quality and relevance of your ad and landing page, and the context of the search. Google Ads gives each keyword a **Quality Score** from 1 to 10, based on expected click-through rate, ad relevance and landing page experience. A relevant, useful ad can beat a bigger bid.

blocks.title: From search to sale with a search ad
items: Customer searches keyword
Auction picks ads
Your ad appears
Customer clicks (you pay)
Landing page converts
blocks.caption: You pay at the click, so the page after the click must do its job.

blocks.text: Keywords and match types

head: Match type
How you write it
What it means
rows: Ads can show for searches related to the meaning, including wider ones. Reaches most people, least control.
Searches that include the meaning of the phrase, such as 'cake delivery in Ikeja'.
Searches with the same meaning as the keyword. Most control, fewest searches.
Stops your ad showing when the search contains this word, so you do not pay for people looking for cake recipes.

blocks.text: For a small budget, start with a handful of phrase and exact match keywords that show buying intent, such as 'order', 'delivery', 'price' or a location. Add negative keywords for searches you do not want: 'free', 'recipe', 'jobs', 'training' or 'how to', unless those are your business.
Writing the ad

Google's standard text format is the **responsive search ad**: you supply up to 15 headlines (30 characters each) and up to 4 descriptions (90 characters each), and Google tests combinations. Include the keyword, a clear benefit, a reason to trust you and a call to action. Set **location targeting** to the area you actually serve, so you do not pay for clicks from people you cannot deliver to.

items: Headline ideas: 'Birthday Cakes in Ikeja', 'Same-Day Delivery Available', 'Order on WhatsApp Today'.
Description idea: 'Custom cakes baked fresh to order. Prices from about ₦25,000. Delivery across Ikeja and Maryland.'
Landing page: the page must show what the ad promised: photos, prices, delivery areas and a clear order button or WhatsApp link.

blocks.title: Worked example: what will a budget buy?
blocks.context: For example, Ronke sets a daily budget of about ₦5,000 for 20 days of a test campaign in Ikeja. Costs per click vary widely by industry and competition, so she uses her own results, not a guess. All figures are illustrative.
steps: Total budget = ₦5,000 × 20 days = ₦100,000.
After the first week her report shows an average cost per click (CPC) of about ₦125. Clicks she can expect = ₦100,000 ÷ ₦125 = 800 clicks.
Her landing page converts 3% of visitors into orders (24 orders from her first 800 visitors in a similar earlier test). Expected orders = 800 × 0.03 = 24.
Cost per order = ₦100,000 ÷ 24 = about ₦4,167.
Her average profit per cake, before advertising, is about ₦9,000. Profit after ad cost per order = ₦9,000 − ₦4,167 = about ₦4,833.
blocks.result: The campaign is profitable, so Ronke keeps it running. If her conversion rate fell to 1%, she would get only 8 orders, costing ₦12,500 each, more than her profit per cake. That is why the landing page matters as much as the ad.

blocks.text: Start small and learn. Run a short test with a few tightly chosen keywords, check the **search terms report** in Google Ads after a few days to see the actual searches that triggered your ads, and add any wasteful ones as negative keywords. Pause keywords that spend money without producing enquiries. Only increase the budget when your cost per order is comfortably below your profit per sale.

blocks.title: How Google spends your daily budget
blocks.text: Google's help pages explain that on some days it may spend up to twice your average daily budget when there are more searches, but over a month it will not charge more than your daily budget multiplied by the average number of days in a month. Check your billing settings before you start and set an end date for tests.

blocks.title: Beware fake 'Google agents'
blocks.text: Google does not call or WhatsApp small businesses to demand payment for keeping their listing or ranking. Make payments only inside your own Google Ads account at ads.google.com, and never share your login or verification codes.

takeaways: Search ads charge per click and appear for keywords you choose.
Ad position depends on bid and quality, not money alone.
Use specific, buying-intent keywords, location targeting and negative keywords.
Cost per order = total spend ÷ orders; it must be below your profit per sale.

activity.title: Plan a small search campaign on paper
steps: List 8 buying-intent keywords for your business and choose a match type for each.
List at least 5 negative keywords.
Write 3 headlines (30 characters or fewer) and 1 description (90 characters or fewer).
Using a test daily budget you can afford and an assumed CPC, calculate expected clicks, orders and cost per order.
activity.evidence: Your keyword sheet, ad text and budget calculation.

lessons.title: Tracking results: analytics, UTM links and a simple dashboard
objectives: Name the key reports in Google Analytics, Search Console and social insights
Tell the difference between vanity metrics and decision metrics
Build a UTM-tagged link to track where visitors come from
Keep a weekly tracking sheet that connects marketing to sales

blocks.text: Marketing without measurement is like cooking without tasting. Each platform gives you free numbers. The skill is knowing which ones to watch, and joining them up so you can see which channel actually brings paying customers.

blocks.name: analytics
blocks.alt: A dashboard with charts and graphs on a screen
blocks.caption: A few well-chosen numbers, checked weekly, beat a hundred numbers checked never.

blocks.text: Where your numbers come from

head: Tool
What it tells you
Key numbers
rows: What visitors do on your website
Users, sessions, engagement rate, traffic sources, key events such as purchases or form sends
How your site appears in Google Search
Search queries, impressions, clicks, click-through rate, average position
How people interact with your listing
Profile views, calls, direction requests, website clicks
How your posts and ads perform
Reach, impressions, engagement, link clicks, messages
Orders, revenue, where each customer heard about you

blocks.text: In GA4, a **session** is one visit; one person can make several. A **key event** is an action you mark as important, such as a purchase, a contact form or a click on your WhatsApp button. The **Traffic acquisition** report shows which sources (Google search, Facebook, direct, email) brought sessions and key events.
Vanity metrics vs decision metrics

blocks.title: Which numbers deserve your attention?
items: Vanity metrics
Decision metrics
blocks.caption: Vanity numbers can rise while sales fall; decision numbers tell you what to change.

blocks.text: UTM links: labelling your traffic

If you share your website link on Instagram, in a WhatsApp broadcast and in an email, how will you know which one brought the visitor? Add **UTM parameters**: small labels at the end of a link that analytics tools read. The three main ones are **utm_source** (where: instagram), **utm_medium** (what type: social, email) and **utm_campaign** (which promotion: easter_sale). Google offers a free Campaign URL Builder that assembles the link for you.

blocks.title: Worked example: tracking an Easter promotion
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells skincare from her website and promotes an Easter offer on three channels.
steps: Instagram bio link: yoursite.com/easter?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=easter_sale
WhatsApp broadcast link: the same, but with utm_source=whatsapp&utm_medium=messaging
Email link: utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email
After two weeks, GA4 shows: Instagram 600 sessions and 12 purchases; WhatsApp 150 sessions and 9 purchases; email 200 sessions and 8 purchases.
Conversion rates: Instagram 12 ÷ 600 = 2%; WhatsApp 9 ÷ 150 = 6%; email 8 ÷ 200 = 4%.
blocks.result: Instagram brought the most visitors, but WhatsApp converted three times better. Ngozi decides to grow her WhatsApp broadcast list (with permission) and keep Instagram for awareness.

blocks.title: No website? Ask every customer
blocks.text: Many Nigerian small businesses sell entirely through WhatsApp, so analytics tools cannot see the sale. Ask every new customer, 'How did you hear about us?' and record the answer. In WhatsApp Business, use labels such as 'From Instagram' or 'From Google' to tag new chats. This simple habit is often the most valuable data you will have.
Your weekly tracking sheet

Create a sheet in Google Sheets or Excel, or a notebook page, with one row per week. Columns: people reached, profile or page visits, messages received, orders, revenue, money spent on ads, and the top source of new customers. Add two calculated columns: **chat-to-order rate** (orders ÷ messages × 100) and **cost per order** (ad spend ÷ orders from ads). Fill it every Monday for the previous week. After a month you will see trends that no single post can show.

Look for change over time, not single days. One quiet Tuesday means little; four weeks of falling messages means something. When a number moves, ask why, and write your guess in a notes column: a holiday, a price change, a new post style. Over time this notes column becomes your own marketing textbook.
A simple weekly review routine

items: Every Monday, open your sheet and your platform insights and fill in last week's row (about 15 minutes).
Compare with the week before and the same week last month. Mark any number that moved by a lot.
Find the channel that brought the most orders, not the most views, and note it.
Write one decision for this week, for example 'Post the menu on Status at 5pm instead of 9pm' or 'Pause the ad with the lowest click-through rate'.
Next Monday, check whether that decision changed the number you expected.

blocks.title: Numbers will never be perfect
blocks.text: Some customers see your Instagram post, search your name on Google a week later and then message you on WhatsApp. No tool records that whole journey. Accept that your data is approximate, and look for clear, repeated patterns rather than exact figures.
Keep your sheet private: it may contain customer names and phone numbers, which are personal data. Share only totals, not contact details, with anyone who helps you with marketing.

takeaways: GA4, Search Console, Business Profile and Meta insights are free sources of data.
Watch decision metrics such as messages, orders and cost per order.
UTM links show which channel brought each website visitor.
Without a website, ask every customer how they heard about you and record it weekly.

activity.title: Set up your tracking
steps: Create a weekly tracking sheet with the columns listed in this lesson.
Build one UTM link for a channel you use and test that it opens correctly.
Add 'How did you hear about us?' to your order conversation for every new customer.
Fill in last week's row as best you can from your records and insights.
activity.evidence: Your tracking sheet with at least one completed week and one UTM link.

quiz.q: Ronke's new website page is not appearing in Google at all. Which stage has most likely failed?
quiz.explain: A page that does not appear at all has usually not been crawled or indexed yet. Submitting it in Search Console and linking to it from other pages helps.

quiz.q: Which search shows transactional intent?
quiz.explain: 'Order' and 'delivery' show the person is ready to buy now.

quiz.q: Halima wants more Google reviews. Which action follows Google's rules?
options: Offer 10% off to clients who post a 5-star review
Ask her sister to post reviews
Send happy clients the review link and ask for an honest review
quiz.explain: Asking real customers for honest reviews is allowed. Incentives, fake reviews and bought reviews break Google's policies.

quiz.q: A search ad campaign spent ₦60,000 and produced 400 clicks and 10 orders. What was the cost per order?
quiz.explain: Cost per order = ₦60,000 ÷ 10 = ₦6,000. (₦150 is the cost per click.)

quiz.q: A baker who only sells cakes keeps paying for clicks from people searching 'cake recipe'. What should she add?
quiz.explain: A negative keyword stops the ad showing for searches containing that word.

quiz.q: Which of these is a decision metric rather than a vanity metric?
quiz.explain: Cost per order connects marketing spend to sales and tells you whether to continue a campaign.

quiz.q: In a UTM link, which parameter tells you the promotion name, such as easter_sale?
quiz.explain: utm_campaign names the promotion; utm_source is where the click came from and utm_medium is the type of channel.

modules.title: Content, social media, email and WhatsApp
modules.overview: Content is what you say; channels are where you say it. This module shows you how to plan useful content, choose and use social platforms with purpose, build an email list with permission, and turn WhatsApp from a chat app into an organised sales tool.

lessons.title: Content marketing: pillars, formats and a content calendar
objectives: Explain what content marketing is and how it moves people through the funnel
Choose three to four content pillars for your business
Turn one idea into several formats
Plan a two-week content calendar you can actually keep

blocks.text: **Content marketing** means attracting and keeping customers by sharing useful, interesting or entertaining material, rather than only shouting 'buy now'. A tailor who posts a short video on 'how to measure yourself for a gown' teaches something useful, shows her skill and reminds viewers she exists. When they need a gown, they think of her first.

blocks.name: content-creator
blocks.alt: A woman recording content on a phone with a ring light
blocks.caption: Useful content builds trust long before a customer is ready to buy.

blocks.text: Content pillars

**Content pillars** are three or four themes you return to again and again. They stop you staring at your phone wondering what to post, and they make sure your content serves every stage of the funnel. Here is a set that works for most small businesses.

head: Pillar
Purpose
Funnel stage
Examples for a hair salon
rows: Solve a small problem for free
How to protect braids at night; how long box braids should stay in
Let people see how you work
Time-lapse of a cornrow style; your clean, organised station
Before-and-after photos (with permission); client voice notes; Google reviews
This week's price list; open slots for Saturday; a mid-week discount

blocks.text: Many marketers suggest that most posts should give value and only a minority should sell directly. Treat that as a rule of thumb, not a law. If every post is an advert, people stop watching. If none of them sell, people enjoy your posts but never know how to buy.
One idea, many formats

Creating content takes time, so get more from each idea. This is called **repurposing**. Formats include short vertical videos (Reels on Instagram and Facebook, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, WhatsApp Status), photos and carousels (several images in one post), text posts, voice notes, live videos, longer YouTube videos and blog articles. Short vertical video is currently a strong format on most social platforms, but photos and text still work, especially on WhatsApp and Facebook.

blocks.title: Worked example: repurposing one idea five ways
blocks.context: For example, Halima's salon gets the same question every week: 'How do I make my braids last longer?'
steps: She records a 45-second vertical video at the salon, showing three tips: wrap with a satin scarf, moisturise the scalp lightly, avoid heavy oils.
She posts the video as an Instagram Reel and a TikTok, with the caption starting 'Want your braids to last 6 weeks? Do these 3 things.'
She shares the same video on WhatsApp Status that evening.
She turns the three tips into a 4-slide photo carousel for Facebook.
She saves the tips as a quick reply in WhatsApp Business, so when clients ask after appointments, she sends them in one tap.
blocks.result: One hour of work produced five pieces of content across four channels, all on her 'Teach' pillar. Her 'Sell' post that week links back: 'Book your braids before Saturday, and we will show you how to keep them neat.'

blocks.text: Your content calendar

A **content calendar** is a simple plan of what you will post, where and when. It can be a table in a notebook or Google Sheets. Batch your work: take photos and record videos on one day, write captions on another, and schedule posts in advance. **Meta Business Suite**, free from Meta, lets you schedule Facebook and Instagram posts ahead of time.

blocks.title: A realistic weekly content rhythm
items: Monday: Teach (short video)
Wednesday: Show (behind the scenes)
Friday: Prove (review or result)
Sunday: Sell (offer and prices)
blocks.caption: Four planned posts a week, one per pillar, is sustainable for most busy owners.

blocks.text: Writing captions that work

items: Open with a hook in the first line, because that is often all people see before tapping 'more': a question, a number or a clear benefit.
Give the useful part quickly, in short sentences.
End with one clear **call to action**: 'Send us a WhatsApp message', 'Tap the link in our bio', 'Save this for later'.
Use a few relevant hashtags or location tags where the platform uses them, such as your city.
Use your customers' own words from your interviews in Lesson 1.2.

blocks.title: Permission and copyright
blocks.text: Ask clients before posting their faces or before-and-after photos, and respect a 'no'. Do not use other people's photos, videos or music as your own. Use your own photos, and for music use the licensed sound libraries inside the apps, which are made for that purpose.

Review your content once a month. In your insights, sort posts by saves, shares and the messages they produced, not only by likes. Look at the top three and ask what they have in common: a pillar, a format, a time of day, a type of hook. Make more of that, and quietly drop formats that took a lot of effort and brought nothing. Your calendar should change as you learn what your own customers respond to.

takeaways: Content marketing attracts customers by being useful, not only by selling.
Three or four content pillars, such as Teach, Show, Prove and Sell, cover the funnel.
Repurpose one idea into several formats to save time.
A simple calendar and batching make consistent posting possible.

activity.title: Plan two weeks of content
steps: Write your three or four content pillars and one sentence on what each means for your business.
List the five questions customers ask you most; each is a 'Teach' idea.
Fill a two-week calendar with at least three posts a week, naming pillar, format and channel.
Create and post the first piece using the caption steps.
activity.evidence: Your content pillars, two-week calendar and a screenshot of the first post.

lessons.title: Social media as a marketing channel
objectives: Choose the right social platforms for your target customer
Set up business or professional accounts to access insights
Calculate engagement rate and interpret reach and impressions
Manage comments and messages in a way that builds trust

blocks.text: Social media lets you reach customers where they already spend time, for free, and later with paid ads. But each platform has its own style and audience, and trying to be everywhere at once usually leads to tired owners and abandoned pages. Choose deliberately.

blocks.name: social-media
blocks.alt: Social media profile cards with likes and comments around a phone
blocks.caption: Each platform has its own style; match the platform to your customer.

blocks.text: Choosing platforms

head: Platform
Strong for
Content style
Good fit for
rows: Local groups, community pages, marketplace, ads to wide age ranges
Most consumer businesses, especially older customers
Discovery by people who do not follow you yet
Products that look interesting in action

blocks.title: Where to focus first
items: Customers here, hard for you: learn it
Customers here, easy for you: focus now
Customers absent, hard for you: skip
Customers absent, easy for you: optional
blocks.caption: Start with the platform where your customers are and you can create content comfortably.

blocks.text: Set up for business

Use a Facebook **Page** (not a personal profile) for your business, and switch Instagram and TikTok to a **business** or **professional** account. These are free and unlock **insights**: data on who sees your content, when your followers are online and which posts perform. They also let you add contact buttons, such as a WhatsApp button, and run ads later. Use the same name, logo and bio across platforms, with your wa.me link.
Reading the numbers

items: **Reach**: the number of different people who saw your content.
**Impressions** (Meta increasingly calls these **views**): the number of times it was shown, including repeats. Impressions are usually higher than reach.
**Engagement**: likes, comments, shares and saves. Saves and shares are especially valuable, because they show people found it useful enough to keep or pass on.
**Engagement rate**: engagements ÷ reach × 100. Platforms and tools define it slightly differently, so compare your own posts using the same formula each time.

blocks.title: Worked example: which post did better?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka compares two posts from her small chops page in Port Harcourt.
steps: Post A, a photo of a platter: reach 2,000; 60 likes, 10 comments, 5 shares, 5 saves = 80 engagements.
Engagement rate A = 80 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 4%.
Post B, a short video packing an order: reach 1,200; 70 likes, 25 comments, 15 shares, 10 saves = 120 engagements.
Engagement rate B = 120 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 10%.
She also checks messages: Post A led to 3 WhatsApp enquiries, Post B to 9.
blocks.result: Post B reached fewer people but engaged far more, and brought three times the enquiries. Amaka plans more 'behind the scenes' packing videos and tracks whether the pattern holds over several weeks.

blocks.text: Community management

Social media is social. Reply to comments and direct messages quickly, ideally the same day. Answer price questions openly or move them politely to WhatsApp with a link; many customers are put off by 'Check DM' with no answer. Thank people who share your posts. Handle complaints calmly: acknowledge, apologise where appropriate, and offer to resolve in private. Delete spam and scam comments, especially fake accounts offering loans or 'customer support', which target your followers.

blocks.title: Watch for impersonators
blocks.text: Scammers sometimes copy a business's name and photos to create a fake page and collect payments. Tell customers clearly in your bio which account numbers and payment links are genuinely yours, ask followers to report fake pages, and report them to the platform yourself.
Profile checklist for any platform

items: A clear profile picture: your logo, or your face if you are the brand. It must be readable at small size.
A bio that says what you sell, where, and how to order, for example 'Small chops and finger foods for parties in Port Harcourt. Order on WhatsApp below.'
A contact button or link: your wa.me link, phone number or link page.
Pinned or highlighted posts showing prices, reviews and how delivery works, so new visitors do not have to scroll.
The same business name and handle on every platform where possible, so people can find you easily.

blocks.text: Finally, be consistent rather than constant. Three thoughtful posts a week, every week, build more trust than twenty posts in one excited week followed by a month of silence. Check your insights to find the days and times your followers are most active, and schedule posts for then.

Join the conversation beyond your own page too. Local Facebook groups for your area, estate or profession often allow business posts on certain days. Read the group rules first, contribute helpful answers, and only then share your offer. A helpful reply in a busy community group can bring more enquiries than a week of posts on a page with few followers.

takeaways: Focus on one or two platforms where your customers are and you can create comfortably.
Business and professional accounts unlock free insights and contact buttons.
Engagement rate = engagements ÷ reach × 100; compare posts with the same formula.
Reply quickly, handle complaints calmly and protect followers from impersonators.

activity.title: Choose and set up your main platform
steps: Place each platform in the four-box matrix for your business and pick your main one.
Convert to a business or professional account and complete the bio with your wa.me link.
Post three times this week following your content calendar.
Calculate the engagement rate of each post and note enquiries from each.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your business profile and a small table of reach, engagement rate and enquiries for three posts.

lessons.title: Email marketing: building a list and sending a newsletter
objectives: Explain why an email list is valuable owned media
Collect email addresses with clear consent
Write a newsletter with a strong subject line and one call to action
Calculate and interpret open, click and unsubscribe rates

blocks.text: Social platforms can change their rules, reduce your reach or suspend an account overnight. An **email list** is different: it is owned media, a list of people who have asked to hear from you. Email suits businesses with customers who use email regularly, such as professionals, organisations, training providers, online shops and anyone selling to other businesses.

blocks.name: email-campaign
blocks.alt: An envelope with a campaign message flying out of a laptop
blocks.caption: An email list is a channel you own and control.

blocks.text: Build the list with permission

Never buy email lists or add people without asking. It is disrespectful, damages your reputation with email providers so your messages land in spam, and conflicts with data protection principles. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 requires a lawful basis, such as consent, for processing personal data. Ask clearly, say what you will send and how often, and make leaving easy.

items: A sign-up form on your website or link page, created with your email tool.
A tick-box on your order form: 'Send me monthly tips and offers by email' (not ticked in advance).
A **lead magnet**: something useful given in exchange for an email address, such as a price guide, a recipe booklet or a checklist.
At events and in your shop: a paper sign-up sheet that states what people are signing up for.

blocks.text: Choose a tool

Use an **email marketing service** rather than your personal Gmail. Examples include Mailchimp, Brevo and MailerLite; most offer free starter plans with limits on contacts or sends, so check the current terms on their sites. These tools provide sign-up forms, templates that display well on phones, an automatic **unsubscribe link** in every email, and reports. Many let you send a **welcome email** automatically when someone joins.

blocks.title: A simple email journey
items: Sign-up with consent
Automatic welcome email
Regular useful newsletter
Occasional clear offer
blocks.caption: Give value first and regularly, and offers are welcomed rather than ignored.

blocks.text: Writing a good newsletter

items: **Subject line**: short and specific, telling the reader what is inside. 'Three ways to store your ankara so colours last' beats 'Newsletter No. 4'.
**Preview text**: the line shown after the subject in many inboxes; use it to add a reason to open.
**Body**: greet by first name if you have it, give one main useful item, keep paragraphs short, and add one or two good photos.
**One call to action**: a single clear button such as 'Shop the new collection' or 'Book a fitting'.
**Footer**: your business name, contact details and the unsubscribe link (your tool adds it).
Send a test to yourself and read it on your phone before sending to everyone.

blocks.text: Email numbers

head: Metric
Formula
What it tells you
rows: Interest in your subject line, but treat it with caution (see note)
Whether the content and call to action worked
Whether you send too often or off-topic
Emails that could not be delivered ÷ emails sent × 100
Whether your list has wrong or old addresses

blocks.title: Why open rates are less reliable now
blocks.text: Some email apps, notably Apple Mail with its Mail Privacy Protection feature, load email content automatically, which can count as an 'open' even if the person never read it. Clicks and sales are more trustworthy measures of success.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a newsletter report
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sends her skincare newsletter to 800 subscribers.
steps: Delivered: 784 (16 bounced). Bounce rate = 16 ÷ 800 × 100 = 2%. She removes the bounced addresses.
Clicks on 'Shop the Easter set': 47. Click rate = 47 ÷ 784 × 100 = about 6%.
Orders from those clicks (tracked with a UTM link): 8. Conversion rate from click to order = 8 ÷ 47 × 100 = about 17%.
Unsubscribes: 4. Unsubscribe rate = 4 ÷ 784 × 100 = about 0.5%.
Revenue: 8 orders × about ₦12,000 = about ₦96,000, from an email that cost her only time.
blocks.result: The email performed well. Ngozi keeps a monthly schedule and tests a different subject line style next month to see if clicks improve.

blocks.text: How often to send

Choose a rhythm you can keep, such as monthly or every two weeks, and tell subscribers at sign-up. Consistency matters more than frequency: a list that hears from you every month remembers who you are, while a list you contact once a year tends to ignore or report the email as spam. Clean your list a few times a year by removing addresses that bounce, and consider a polite 'Do you still want to hear from us?' email to people who have not clicked anything in a long time. A smaller, interested list is worth more than a large, silent one.

blocks.title: Combine email with WhatsApp
blocks.text: Many Nigerian customers check WhatsApp more often than email. When you send a newsletter, post a short Status with the main tip and a link to the full version. Each channel then supports the other.

takeaways: An email list is owned media that no platform can take away.
Collect addresses only with clear consent and make unsubscribing easy.
Use a proper email tool, one main message and one call to action.
Judge emails by clicks and sales more than by open rate.

activity.title: Start your email list
steps: Create a free account on an email marketing tool.
Make a sign-up form and write a consent line saying what you will send and how often.
Write a short welcome email with one useful tip.
Share the sign-up form with existing customers and record how many join in one week.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your sign-up form, your welcome email text and your subscriber count.

lessons.title: WhatsApp marketing: catalog, labels, Status and broadcasts
objectives: Set up the main sales features of WhatsApp Business
Use labels to track customers through the funnel
Use Status and broadcast lists with permission and without spamming
Protect yourself and your customers from common WhatsApp scams

blocks.text: For many Nigerian small businesses, WhatsApp is where the sale actually happens. Customers find you on Instagram or Google, then tap through to chat, ask the price, send a transfer receipt and arrange delivery. **WhatsApp Business**, the free business version of the app from Meta, turns this from a messy pile of chats into an organised sales channel.

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.alt: A seller and a customer exchanging chat messages on phones
blocks.caption: On WhatsApp, the conversation is often where the sale is won or lost.

blocks.text: Key features and how to use them

head: Feature
What it does
How to use it well
rows: Shows address, hours, description, email, website
Fill every field; match your Google profile
A product showcase inside WhatsApp with photos, prices and descriptions
Add your best sellers with clear photos and prices; share items straight into chats
Sent automatically when a customer messages you for the first time or after a period of no contact
Welcome them, say what to expect and point to the catalog
Give your hours and when you will reply
Saved answers you send by typing / and a shortcut
Save prices, delivery fees, account details, care instructions
Track where each customer is in the funnel
A link or scannable code that opens a chat with you
Put it on social bios, flyers, packaging and receipts

blocks.text: Labels as a mini sales pipeline

blocks.title: Labelling chats through the funnel
items: New enquiry
Price sent
Paid
Delivered
Repeat customer
blocks.caption: Labels show at a glance who needs a follow-up and who is ready for a thank-you.

blocks.text: Once a day, open the 'Price sent' label. These are people who asked but did not buy. A friendly follow-up, once, often recovers sales: 'Hi Chioma, just checking if you would like to go ahead with the two Ankara gowns? I have your size in stock until Friday.' Then stop. Repeated chasing annoys people.
Status and broadcast lists

**Status** updates disappear after 24 hours and are seen by contacts who have your number saved. They are ideal for daily menus, new arrivals and short videos. **Broadcast lists** send one message to many contacts at once, but each person receives it as a private chat, and only contacts who have **saved your number** in their phone receive it. That rule protects people from spam, so always ask customers to save your number.

blocks.title: Worked example: a weekly WhatsApp routine
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs her Abuja meal-prep sales through WhatsApp Business. She has 180 customers who have saved her number and agreed to receive her weekly menu.
steps: Sunday 2pm: she posts the week's menu on Status as three photos and one 20-second video of the cooking.
Sunday 4pm: she sends the menu to her broadcast list with the message 'This week's menu is here! Reply with your order by 8pm. Reply STOP if you no longer want the menu.'
She receives 42 replies. Response rate = 42 ÷ 180 × 100 = about 23%. 31 of them order. Conversion rate = 31 ÷ 42 × 100 = about 74%.
She labels each chat 'Paid' once the transfer is confirmed in her bank app, never from a screenshot alone.
Two people reply STOP. She removes them from the list immediately.
blocks.result: Bisi earns most of her weekly orders from one organised Sunday routine. Her high conversion rate shows that people on a permission-based list are warm buyers.

blocks.title: Do not spam
blocks.text: Adding strangers to groups or messaging people who never contacted you leads to blocks and reports, and WhatsApp may restrict accounts that receive many of them. Message only people who have contacted you or agreed to hear from you, and always honour a request to stop.

blocks.title: Common WhatsApp scams
blocks.text: Never share the six-digit WhatsApp code sent by SMS: whoever has it can take your account. Confirm payments in your bank or payment app, not from a screenshot, because fake transfer receipts are easy to make. Be careful with 'customers' who overpay and ask for a refund of the difference. Turn on two-step verification in Settings, Account.
Writing messages customers welcome

items: Reply fast. A customer asking the price is comparing sellers; the first clear reply often wins. Quick replies help.
Answer the actual question first: the price, then the details. Hiding the price makes people leave.
Send the catalog item or a photo, the price, the delivery fee and the time, in one tidy message.
Use the customer's name, and keep a warm, respectful tone, even when someone haggles hard.
After delivery, send a thank-you and, a few days later, ask how they found it. That is the moment to share your Google review link.

blocks.text: As you grow, Meta also offers **click-to-WhatsApp ads**, which you will meet in Module 4: adverts on Facebook and Instagram whose button opens a WhatsApp chat with you. Businesses with very high message volumes can use the WhatsApp Business Platform through approved providers, but the free app is enough for most small businesses.

takeaways: WhatsApp Business adds a profile, catalog, automatic messages, quick replies and labels.
Use labels as a simple pipeline and follow up once on unpaid enquiries.
Broadcasts reach only people who saved your number; always give a way to stop.
Confirm payments in your bank app and never share your WhatsApp code.

activity.title: Organise your WhatsApp Business
steps: Add at least eight products to your catalog with photos, prices and descriptions.
Write and switch on a greeting message and an away message.
Create five quick replies for your most common questions.
Create the five labels from the diagram and label your last 20 chats.
Send one polite follow-up to each chat labelled 'Price sent'.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your catalog, greeting message and labels, plus a note of how many follow-ups turned into orders.

quiz.q: Halima posts a video showing how to protect braids at night. Which content pillar and funnel stage is this mainly?
quiz.explain: It teaches something useful for free, which attracts new people at the awareness stage.

quiz.q: A post reached 1,500 people and got 45 likes, 15 comments and 15 shares. What is the engagement rate using engagements ÷ reach × 100?
Ngozi wants to grow her email list quickly. Which method is acceptable?
options: Offer a free skincare guide in exchange for signing up, with a clear consent line
Buy a list of 5,000 Lagos email addresses
Add every WhatsApp contact without asking
Pre-tick the newsletter box on her order form
quiz.explain: A lead magnet with clear, freely given consent is fine. Buying lists, adding people without asking and pre-ticked boxes are not genuine consent.

quiz.q: An email went to 500 delivered inboxes and got 25 clicks. What was the click rate?
Bisi's broadcast message did not reach some customers on her list. What is the most likely reason?
options: Those customers have not saved her number
quiz.explain: WhatsApp broadcast messages are delivered only to contacts who have saved your number.

quiz.q: A customer sends a screenshot of a transfer and asks you to dispatch now. What should you do?
options: Dispatch immediately; the screenshot is proof
Confirm the money has arrived in your bank or payment app first
quiz.explain: Fake receipts are easy to create. Always confirm the credit in your own account before dispatching.

modules.title: Campaigns, paid ads, measurement and growth
modules.overview: Now you bring everything together. You will plan a focused campaign, run small paid social ads safely, calculate the metrics that tell you whether you made or lost money, and use testing to grow what works step by step.

lessons.title: Planning a marketing campaign from brief to launch
