objectives: Explain the difference between always-on marketing and a campaign
Write a one-page campaign brief with objective, audience, offer and budget
Create an honest, attractive offer
Plan a campaign timeline from preparation to review

blocks.text: Your weekly posts and WhatsApp routine are **always-on marketing**: steady activity that keeps you visible. A **campaign** is different: a focused push with one objective, a clear offer, a start and end date and a budget. Good moments for campaigns include festive seasons such as Christmas, Eid and Easter, back-to-school, Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, the launch of a new product, or a quiet month you want to fill.

blocks.name: launch-day
blocks.alt: A team celebrating a product launch with a rocket
blocks.caption: A campaign is a planned push with a clear start, end and objective.

blocks.text: The one-page campaign brief

A **campaign brief** is a short document that answers every important question before you spend money. Even if you work alone, writing it forces clear thinking, and if someone helps you (a designer, a friend who runs your ads), it keeps everyone aligned.

head: Section
Question it answers
Example: back-to-school uniforms
rows: What one result do we want, by when?
Parents of primary pupils within 5 km of our shop in Kaduna
Free name embroidery on orders placed before 20 August
What single idea should they remember?
Neat, durable uniforms, ready in 5 days, with names sewn in
WhatsApp Status and broadcast, Facebook ad to parents nearby, school gate flyers
About ₦40,000 ads, ₦10,000 flyers, 6 hours a week
How will we know it worked?
Orders, cost per order, enquiries by source

blocks.text: Making an honest offer

An **offer** gives people a reason to act now rather than later. Good offers include a bonus (free embroidery, free delivery), a bundle (three uniforms for a set price), a deadline, or a limited quantity that is genuinely limited. Calculate the cost first: a 20% discount on a product with a 30% profit margin leaves you with very little. Bonuses that cost you little but are valued highly, such as free name embroidery, often work better than deep discounts.

blocks.title: Keep it truthful
blocks.text: Do not invent fake countdowns, fake 'only 2 left' messages or false 'was ₦20,000, now ₦10,000' prices. Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) protects consumers against misleading claims, and once customers catch one false claim, they stop trusting the rest.
The campaign timeline

blocks.title: Five phases of a four-week campaign
items: Week 0: brief and prepare
Week 1: tease and warm up
Weeks 2 to 3: launch and push
Final days: deadline reminder
After: review results
blocks.caption: Preparation and review are part of the campaign, not extras.

items: **Prepare**: write the brief, take photos, design graphics, write captions and quick replies, check stock, set up UTM links and tracking.
**Tease**: hint at what is coming on Status and social media to build interest.
**Launch and push**: announce the offer on all channels, start ads, follow up enquiries daily.
**Deadline reminder**: one honest reminder 2 or 3 days before the offer ends often brings a burst of orders.
**Review**: compare results with the objective and write down what you learned for next time.

blocks.title: Worked example: splitting the budget and setting targets
blocks.context: For example, Maryam runs the uniform campaign in the brief above. She has about ₦50,000 to spend and a profit of about ₦3,500 per uniform order (illustrative figures).
steps: Break-even cost per order = profit per order = ₦3,500. She wants to keep at least half, so her target cost per order is ₦1,750 or less.
Maximum orders she must win from paid channels to stay on target: ₦50,000 ÷ ₦1,750 = about 29 orders.
Her objective is 60 orders, so she expects about 31 to come from free channels: her broadcast list, Status and returning parents.
She splits money: ₦40,000 to a Facebook and Instagram ad over 3 weeks (about ₦1,900 a day) and ₦10,000 to flyers at two school gates with her WhatsApp QR code.
She adds a question to her order chat, 'Where did you see our offer?', and labels each chat by source.
blocks.result: Maryam knows before she starts what success looks like and the most she can pay per order. At the end she can say exactly which channel delivered.

blocks.text: Prepare your capacity too. A successful campaign can bring more orders than you can fulfil, and late deliveries create bad reviews. Check that you have materials, helpers and delivery arrangements for the number of orders in your objective, plus a little extra.

Finally, decide in advance what you will do if things go wrong. If by the end of week two you have far fewer enquiries than planned, will you change the offer, change the creative or move money to a better channel? Writing this 'if, then' plan in the brief stops you from panicking and spending more on something that is not working.

takeaways: A campaign has one objective, an offer, a start and end date, and a budget.
Write a one-page brief before spending money.
Offers must be honest; calculate their cost before launching.
Set a target cost per order below your profit per order, and track sources.

activity.title: Write your campaign brief
steps: Choose a moment in the next two months for a campaign.
Fill in all seven sections of the brief for your business.
Calculate your break-even and target cost per order.
Draw your timeline with dates for each phase.
activity.evidence: Your completed one-page campaign brief with calculations and timeline.

lessons.title: Running paid social ads: objectives, audiences and budgets
objectives: Describe the campaign, ad set and ad levels in Meta Ads Manager
Choose the right campaign objective for your goal
Define a local audience and a small test budget
Create ad creative that follows platform rules

blocks.text: Paid social ads put your content in front of people who do not follow you yet, chosen by location, age and interests. For most Nigerian small businesses, the main option is **Meta** advertising, which places ads on Facebook, Instagram, Messenger and other Meta placements. TikTok, LinkedIn and others have similar tools; once you understand one, the others feel familiar.

blocks.name: social-strategy
blocks.alt: A person arranging social media ad cards on a board
blocks.caption: Paid social ads reach people who have never heard of you, chosen by location and interests.

blocks.text: Boost or Ads Manager?

The **Boost** button on a Facebook or Instagram post is the quickest way to advertise: you choose a goal, an audience, a budget and a duration. **Meta Ads Manager** (also reachable through Meta Business Suite) gives far more control: more objectives, detailed reporting, testing several ads, and better placement choices. Boosting is fine for a first try; move to Ads Manager once you want to compare and improve.
Three levels of an ad

blocks.title: How Meta organises ads
items: Campaign: objective
Ad set: audience, budget, schedule, placements
Ad: image or video, text, button
blocks.caption: One campaign can hold several ad sets, and each ad set can hold several ads to compare.

head: Objective
Use it when you want
Typical result measured
rows: As many local people as possible to see you
Visits to your website or link page
Messages, video views or post interaction; includes ads that open WhatsApp chats
People to fill a form with their contact details
Purchases on your website (needs tracking set up)

blocks.text: Choose the objective that matches the action you actually want. Meta's system shows your ad to the people it predicts are most likely to take that action. If you choose Awareness but really want WhatsApp orders, you may get cheap reach and very few chats. For most WhatsApp-based sellers, an Engagement campaign with **WhatsApp** as the message destination (a **click-to-WhatsApp ad**) is the natural choice, because the ad button opens a chat with you.
Audience and budget

items: **Location**: the area you can actually serve. You can target cities, or a radius around an address, for example 5 km around your shop.
**Age and gender**: only narrow these if you are sure; your customer profile from Lesson 1.2 helps.
**Detailed targeting**: interests and behaviours, such as 'weddings' or 'parenting'. Meta may widen this automatically if it predicts better results.
**Budget**: daily or lifetime. For a test, choose an amount you can afford to lose entirely while learning, and run it for at least several days so the system has time to learn.
**Payment**: add a payment method in the ad account's billing settings. Check the currency and that your card is enabled for international or online payments with your bank.

blocks.title: Worked example: a small click-to-WhatsApp test
blocks.context: For example, Amaka tests ads for her party small chops in Port Harcourt with about ₦14,000 over 7 days. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Campaign: objective Engagement, conversion location WhatsApp.
Ad set: Port Harcourt, 15 km radius, ages 25 to 50, budget about ₦2,000 per day for 7 days.
Two ads in the same ad set: Ad A, a photo of a full platter; Ad B, a 15-second video of trays being packed.
Results after 7 days: Ad A spent ₦6,500 and started 26 conversations (₦250 each). Ad B spent ₦7,500 and started 50 conversations (₦150 each).
From her labels: Ad A chats produced 4 orders, Ad B chats produced 9. Cost per order: A = ₦6,500 ÷ 4 = ₦1,625; B = ₦7,500 ÷ 9 = about ₦833.
blocks.result: The packing video produced conversations and orders at about half the cost. Amaka switches off Ad A and makes two more videos in the same style to test next week.

blocks.text: Creative that works and gets approved

items: Use real photos or videos of your product, with good light; vertical (9:16) or square formats display well on phones.
Put the main message in the first line of text and the first 3 seconds of video.
Show the price or 'from' price where you can; it filters out people who cannot afford it.
Use a clear button, such as Send WhatsApp message, Shop now or Learn more.
Read Meta's Advertising Standards. Ads are reviewed before running, and some products and claims are restricted, for example health claims, financial services and alcohol.

blocks.title: Avoid ad scams and account theft
blocks.text: Fake 'Meta support' messages warning that your page will be deleted unless you click a link are a common way scammers steal pages and ad accounts. Meta's real notifications appear inside your Meta Business Suite or account settings. Do not click such links, and keep two-step verification on.

takeaways: Meta ads have three levels: campaign (objective), ad set (audience and budget) and ad (creative).
Pick the objective that matches the action you want; click-to-WhatsApp suits chat-based sellers.
Test with a small budget you can afford to lose, over several days.
Compare ads by cost per order, not only cost per click or conversation.

activity.title: Plan or run a small ad test
steps: Choose your campaign objective and write why it fits your goal.
Define your ad set: location, age range, budget and duration.
Create two different ads (different photo or video) for the same offer.
Run the test, or if you are not ready to spend, complete the plan and estimate results using your own past numbers.
activity.evidence: Your ad plan, the two ad creatives and either the results table or your estimate.

lessons.title: Measuring campaign success: the core metrics with worked calculations
objectives: Calculate reach-based metrics: CPM and frequency
Calculate click-through rate and cost per click
Calculate conversion rate, cost per result and return on ad spend
Judge whether a campaign made or lost money using break-even cost per result

blocks.text: Every ad platform throws numbers at you. This lesson gives you the formulas behind the most important ones, so you can calculate them yourself, check reports and compare channels fairly. You only need a calculator on your phone. Follow the numbers down the funnel, from people reached to money made.

blocks.name: abacus
blocks.alt: A wooden abacus with coloured beads
blocks.caption: A few simple calculations tell you whether your marketing made or lost money.

blocks.title: Metrics down the funnel
items: Impressions and reach
Clicks (CTR, CPC)
Conversions (conversion rate)
Cost per result
Revenue (ROAS)
blocks.caption: Each step down the funnel has its own metric; a weak step shows where to improve.

blocks.text: The formulas

head: Metric
Formula
Plain meaning
rows: Count of different people who saw the ad
Count of times the ad was shown
Average times each person saw it
Share of views that became clicks
Share of clicks that took the action you want
Price of each order, lead or chat
Naira of sales for each naira of ads

blocks.text: A **conversion** is whatever action counts as success for that campaign: an order, a booking, a form completed or a WhatsApp chat started. Be clear about which one you mean, because 'cost per result' in Ads Manager means cost per whatever result your campaign objective counts, which may be conversations rather than paid orders.

blocks.title: Worked example: a full campaign report
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi ran a Traffic campaign for her skincare website. Ads Manager and GA4 show the following. Figures are illustrative.
steps: Spend ₦30,000. Impressions 60,000. Reach 20,000.
Frequency = 60,000 ÷ 20,000 = 3. Each person saw the ad 3 times on average.
Purchases (tracked with UTM links in GA4) 18. Conversion rate = 18 ÷ 900 × 100 = 2%. Cost per purchase = ₦30,000 ÷ 18 = about ₦1,667.
Revenue from those purchases ₦216,000 (average order about ₦12,000). ROAS = ₦216,000 ÷ ₦30,000 = 7.2.
blocks.result: Each naira of advertising brought about ₦7.20 in sales. Whether that is profitable depends on her costs, which is the next step.

blocks.text: Revenue is not profit: break-even cost per result

ROAS uses revenue, but you also pay for products, packaging and delivery. Your **break-even cost per result** is the profit you make on one sale before advertising. If your cost per order is below it, the ad made money; above it, the ad lost money on that sale. In Ngozi's case, if each order costs her about ₦7,000 in products, packaging and delivery, her profit before ads is ₦12,000 − ₦7,000 = ₦5,000. Her cost per purchase of about ₦1,667 is well below ₦5,000, so each ad-driven order earned about ₦3,333 after ad costs, a total of about ₦60,000 profit from the campaign.

blocks.title: Break-even ROAS
blocks.text: You can also express break-even as a ROAS: average order value ÷ profit per order before ads. For Ngozi: ₦12,000 ÷ ₦5,000 = 2.4. Any ROAS above 2.4 makes money; below it loses money. Her 7.2 is comfortably above.
Diagnosing problems with the numbers

head: What you see
Likely problem
What to try
rows: The ad does not catch attention or reaches the wrong people
New image or video, stronger first line, tighter audience
The landing page or chat does not convince
Clearer price, faster replies, easier payment, more reviews
Frequency rising above about 4 or 5 with falling results
The same people are tired of the ad
Refresh the creative or widen the audience
Competitive period or very narrow audience
Widen the audience or accept it during peak seasons

blocks.title: Compare like with like
blocks.text: There are no universal 'good' numbers. Rates differ by country, industry, season and format. Compare your campaign against your own earlier campaigns and against your break-even, not against figures quoted online.

The same formulas work without a website or Ads Manager. Suppose you paid ₦8,000 for flyers and ₦4,000 for a WhatsApp Status promotion by a popular local page, and you recorded every new customer's answer to 'Where did you hear about us?'. If flyers brought 4 orders and the promotion brought 6, your cost per order was ₦2,000 for both. Then compare each with your profit per order. Simple records in a notebook are enough to make sound decisions.

takeaways: CTR = clicks ÷ impressions × 100; CPC = spend ÷ clicks.
Conversion rate = conversions ÷ clicks × 100; cost per result = spend ÷ results.
ROAS = revenue ÷ ad spend, but profit needs your product costs too.
If cost per order is below profit per order before ads, the campaign made money.

activity.title: Calculate your own campaign metrics
steps: Take a recent ad, boost or promotion (or use the numbers from Amaka's test in Lesson 4.2).
Record spend, impressions, reach, clicks, results and revenue.
Calculate frequency, CPM, CTR, CPC, conversion rate, cost per result and ROAS.
Work out your profit per order before ads and decide whether the campaign made money.
activity.evidence: A calculation sheet showing every formula, your numbers and your verdict.

lessons.title: Iterating and scaling: testing, learning and growing what works
objectives: Run a fair A/B test that changes one thing at a time
Decide when to stop, keep or scale a campaign using your numbers
Calculate a simple customer lifetime value
Grow through repeat customers and referrals, not only new ads

blocks.text: No marketer gets everything right the first time. The difference between businesses that grow and those that stall is a habit: try something, measure it, keep what works, change what does not, and repeat. This habit is called **iteration**. Done steadily, small improvements at each funnel stage multiply into large gains.

blocks.name: growth-curve
blocks.alt: A rising growth curve with a person climbing it
blocks.caption: Steady testing and learning turn small improvements into real growth.

blocks.title: The test and learn cycle
items: Plan: pick one change
Run: test fairly
Measure: compare numbers
Decide: keep, change or stop
blocks.caption: Go round this cycle every week or two, one change at a time.

blocks.text: A/B testing

An **A/B test** compares two versions that differ in **one** thing only: the image, the headline, the offer, the audience or the posting time. If you change several things at once and results improve, you will not know which change helped. Meta Ads Manager has a built-in A/B test feature, but you can also test manually, as Amaka did with two ads in one ad set, or by alternating two WhatsApp follow-up messages.

items: **Test the big things first**: the offer and the main image or video usually matter more than button colour or small wording changes.

**Give it enough data**: a test with 5 clicks each tells you almost nothing. Wait until each version has had a fair number of results, and run tests for full weeks where possible, because weekdays and weekends behave differently.
**Write it down**: date, what you changed, the numbers and your decision. This log is your playbook.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing an offer
blocks.context: For example, Halima's salon tests two offers for quiet weekdays, each sent to half of her 200-person broadcast list over two weeks.
steps: Version A, sent to 100 clients: '10% off all styles on Tuesday and Wednesday.' Bookings: 8.
Version B, sent to 100 clients: 'Free hot-oil treatment with any style on Tuesday and Wednesday.' Bookings: 14.
Booking rate A = 8 ÷ 100 = 8%. Booking rate B = 14 ÷ 100 = 14%.
Cost per booking: on an average style of about ₦15,000, 10% off costs her ₦1,500 per booking. The hot-oil treatment costs about ₦600 in products and 10 minutes of time.
She repeats the test with a new split the next fortnight; B wins again (13 bookings vs 7).
blocks.result: The free treatment brought more bookings and cost less per booking. Because the result held in a second round, Halima adopts it as her standard weekday offer.

blocks.text: Stop, keep or scale

head: Situation
Decision
rows: Cost per order well above break-even after a fair test
Stop, or change one big thing (offer, creative, audience) and retest
Cost per order below break-even, results steady
Keep running and keep testing new creative
Cost per order well below break-even for several weeks
Scale: raise the budget gradually, and watch cost per order closely
Refresh creative or widen the audience before adding money

blocks.text: **Scale gradually.** Large sudden jumps in budget can unsettle the ad system's learning and push costs up, so raise budgets in steps and check results after each step. Also check your capacity: doubling orders is only good if you can still deliver on time and maintain quality.
Growth beyond ads: lifetime value

Winning a customer once is expensive; keeping her is cheaper. **Customer lifetime value** (CLV) estimates how much profit one customer brings over the whole time she buys from you. A simple version: profit per order × orders per year × years she stays.

items: Example: Bisi's meal packs earn about ₦3,000 profit per order. A typical regular orders twice a month (24 times a year) and stays about 1.5 years.
CLV = ₦3,000 × 24 × 1.5 = ₦108,000 profit (illustrative).
So even paying ₦4,000 in ads to win a new regular customer is worthwhile, although it is more than the profit on her first order, as long as she becomes a regular.
Ways to raise CLV: excellent service, follow-up messages, a simple loyalty reward (for example, every 10th order includes a free dessert), and asking for referrals.

blocks.title: Referrals: your cheapest channel
blocks.text: Ask happy customers directly: 'If you know anyone who would enjoy this, please share my number.' A small thank-you for referrals, given to the customer who refers, is a common and honest practice. Track referrals with a label so you know how many new customers come this way.

Return to your 90-day plan from Lesson 1.4 every month. Update the conversion rates with real numbers, move effort towards the channels with the lowest cost per order and the highest repeat rate, and set the next goal. That loop of plan, act, measure and improve is digital marketing.

takeaways: Change one thing at a time in an A/B test and give it enough data.
Use cost per order against break-even to stop, keep or scale.
Scale budgets gradually and check that you can still deliver well.
Customer lifetime value shows why repeat customers and referrals matter.

activity.title: Run one A/B test
steps: Choose one thing to test: an offer, an image, a headline or a posting time.
Create version A and version B that differ only in that one thing.
Run both fairly to similar audiences for at least one full week.
Record results, calculate the rate for each version and write your decision.
Calculate the lifetime value of a typical customer for your business.
activity.evidence: Your test log with both versions, results, calculations, decision and CLV calculation.

quiz.q: Maryam earns about ₦3,500 profit per order before ads. Her campaign spent ₦28,000 and produced 10 orders. What should she conclude?
options: The campaign lost money on every order
Each order cost ₦2,800, more than her profit per order
Each order cost ₦2,800, so it made about ₦700 profit per order
quiz.explain: Cost per order = ₦28,000 ÷ 10 = ₦2,800, below her ₦3,500 break-even, leaving about ₦700 per order. Profitable, but thin; she should test to lower the cost.

quiz.q: Amaka sells mostly through WhatsApp chats. Which Meta campaign objective fits best?
options: Engagement with WhatsApp as the destination
Sales on a website she does not have
quiz.explain: A click-to-WhatsApp ad under the Engagement objective opens a chat, which is where her sales happen.

quiz.q: An ad had 40,000 impressions and 600 clicks. What is the click-through rate?
Spend ₦20,000, revenue from ads ₦90,000. What is the ROAS?
quiz.explain: ROAS = ₦90,000 ÷ ₦20,000 = 4.5. Each naira of ads brought ₦4.50 in sales.

quiz.q: Halima wants to know whether a new photo improves bookings. In her A/B test she should:
options: Change only the photo and keep everything else the same
Change the photo, headline and offer together
Send version A on Christmas Eve and version B in January
quiz.explain: A fair test changes one variable at a time, under similar conditions, with enough data.

quiz.q: Many clicks but very few orders usually points to a problem with:
options: The landing page or chat that follows the click
quiz.explain: If people click but do not buy, the ad is working; the page or conversation after the click needs improving.

quiz.q: A regular customer brings ₦2,000 profit per order, orders 12 times a year and stays 2 years. What is her lifetime value?

finalQuiz.q: Which order correctly lists the four funnel stages used in this course?
finalQuiz.explain: People first discover you (awareness), compare and ask (consideration), buy (conversion) and then return and refer (loyalty).

finalQuiz.q: Tola wants 50 orders next month. 25% of her chats become orders, and 5% of people who see her posts send a chat. How many people must she reach?
Which is the strongest value proposition?
options: Quality cakes at the best prices
We are the number one bakery
Custom birthday cakes for Ikeja families, baked fresh and delivered within 3 hours
finalQuiz.explain: It names the customer, the result and a specific difference. The others are vague or unprovable.

finalQuiz.q: Funke works from home and visits clients to take measurements. How should she set up her Google Business Profile address?
options: Leave the profile without any location
Use a busy market address so more people see it
Hide her home address and set a service area
Use a different business name to rank higher
finalQuiz.explain: Service-area businesses can hide their address and list the areas they serve. Fake addresses and keyword-stuffed names break Google's guidelines.

finalQuiz.q: Which Google tool shows which searches led people to see and click on your website?
finalQuiz.explain: Search Console reports search queries, impressions, clicks, CTR and average position for your site.

finalQuiz.q: A UTM link shows Instagram brought 500 sessions and 5 sales, and WhatsApp brought 100 sessions and 4 sales. Which statement is right?
options: Instagram converts better because it brought more sessions
finalQuiz.explain: Instagram: 5 ÷ 500 = 1%. WhatsApp: 4 ÷ 100 = 4%. More visitors does not mean better conversion.

finalQuiz.q: What is the main purpose of content pillars?
options: To post the same message every day
To give you a few repeatable themes that cover every funnel stage
finalQuiz.explain: Pillars such as Teach, Show, Prove and Sell keep content varied, consistent and connected to the funnel.

finalQuiz.q: Ngozi's newsletter shows a high open rate but almost no clicks. What is the best interpretation?
options: The email was a great success
Opens can be inflated by privacy features, and the content or call to action did not persuade
Her bounce rate is too high
finalQuiz.explain: Open rates are unreliable because some apps auto-load emails. Clicks show whether the content and call to action worked.

finalQuiz.q: Which WhatsApp practice is both effective and respectful?
options: Adding all your phone contacts to a sales group
Sending one polite follow-up to customers labelled 'Price sent'
Messaging the same unpaid customer every day
finalQuiz.explain: One friendly follow-up recovers sales without spamming. Mass adds, repeated chasing and sharing data damage trust and can get your account restricted.

finalQuiz.q: In Meta Ads Manager, where do you set the audience location and budget?
finalQuiz.explain: The campaign holds the objective, the ad set holds audience, budget, schedule and placements, and the ad holds the creative.

finalQuiz.q: An ad spent ₦15,000, got 300 clicks and 12 orders. Profit per order before ads is ₦1,000. What should the seller conclude?
options: Profitable: 12 orders is a good number
Losing money: cost per order is ₦1,250, above the ₦1,000 profit
finalQuiz.explain: Cost per order = ₦15,000 ÷ 12 = ₦1,250, which is more than the ₦1,000 profit per order, so each ad-driven order loses about ₦250 unless those customers buy again.

finalQuiz.q: Halima's ad has run for three weeks; frequency has climbed to 6 and cost per booking is rising. What should she do first?
options: Refresh the creative or widen the audience
finalQuiz.explain: High frequency with falling results suggests ad fatigue. New creative or a wider audience usually helps more than extra money.

capstone.title: My 90-day digital marketing plan and first campaign report
capstone.brief: Produce a practical marketing portfolio for your own business: a customer profile, a completed digital presence, a 90-day plan with funnel calculations, a campaign brief, and a results report with the core metrics calculated and a clear decision on what to do next.
steps: Write your customer profile and value proposition based on at least three customer conversations (Lesson 1.2).
Complete your starter kit: WhatsApp Business profile and catalog, Google Business Profile and one social account, with consistent name, address and phone number (Lessons 1.3, 2.2, 3.4).
Write a SMART 90-day goal and work backwards through the funnel to the reach you need (Lesson 1.4).
Plan two weeks of content using your pillars and publish it (Lessons 3.1, 3.2).
Write a one-page campaign brief with offer, budget, break-even and target cost per order (Lesson 4.1).
Run the campaign, free or paid, tracking sources with labels, UTM links or 'How did you hear about us?' (Lessons 2.4, 4.2).

Calculate reach, CTR, conversion rate, cost per result and ROAS where available, compare with break-even, and write your stop, keep or scale decision plus one A/B test for next time (Lessons 4.3, 4.4).
evidence: Customer profile, value proposition and interview notes
Screenshots of your WhatsApp Business profile, catalog, Google Business Profile and social bio
Two-week content calendar and screenshots of published posts
Results sheet with every formula shown and a written decision
A/B test plan for your next campaign
